documents.abstract: Reports safe arrival in Rostock, plans to winter in the Jurists' College for observations, and urges the recipient to keep the reasons for his departure secret.
Acknowledges a letter of consolation on his father's death and reflects on theological and philosophical sources of comfort available to him.
Acknowledges three letters from Tycho, congratulates him on newfound independence after his father's death, and offers cautious advice on a planned threefold journey.
Responds with playful alchemical and Neoplatonic imagery to praise the extemporaneous quality of Tycho's writing, comparing its heat to solar and divine inspiration.
Replies in hendecasyllabic verse cast as prose, expressing delight at Pratensis's letter and lamenting the displacement of true learning by scholastic barbarism.

Reports on the gilding of Tycho's celestial globe — the goldsmith cannot lay gold stars on silver, the painter would smother the engraving — and urges an all-gold scheme with matt figures on a burnished ground, costed at four rose nobles; then on the printing of De nova stella, arguing Tycho out of the title-word Lucubrationes.
Sends a kinsman with greetings and solicits Tycho's opinion on the new star of 1572, noting sharp disagreement among learned men over its nature.
Reports observations of the 1572 Cassiopeia star made with the Augsburg quadrant, finding zero parallax and therefore a supralunary position, despite reluctance to contradict Aristotle.
Reports that a carrier's treachery caused Tycho to miss acquiring Ambrosius's library and Schreckenfuchs's armilla, and offers to help procure the latter.
Reports that Schreckenfuchs's Ptolemaic armillae have been obtained and will be sent with Regiomontanus's treatise on the instrument's construction and use.
Acknowledges receipt of the book *On the New Star* and praises Tycho for restoring astronomy from common neglect to its proper dignity.
Confirms forwarding a sealed box and money to Rostock and expresses eagerness to hear Tycho's news from his recent travels through Germany.
Confirms the Rostock business was handled and reveals a secret plan to depart for Germany, asking Pratensis to share it only with the French Ambassador Dançay.
Expresses joy at the king's gracious invitation for Tycho to remain in Denmark, interpreting it as divine providence, and urges Tycho to accept.
Returns borrowed Greek propositions, mentions forwarding a sundials manuscript, and approves Tycho's resolve to devote himself to celestial observations.
Mourns the death of Pratensis and asks Tycho's guidance on a dedication cornerstone that Pratensis had reserved to himself before his death.
Confirms a dedication stone is ready with the requested inscription and urges Tycho to summon him and invite guests for the ceremony.
Thanks Tycho for the gift of his book on the New Star, congratulates him on safe return to his homeland, and expresses continued regard.
Recalls their meeting at Regensburg and expresses grief at their swift parting, explaining the long delay in writing by lawsuits and pressing occupations.
Responds to two long-unanswered letters, mourning the death of Pratensis and acknowledging Severinus's account of his personal difficulties.
Asks Tycho to intercede with the King or court friends on behalf of a Scottish soldier owed outstanding pay from the Danish-Swedish war.
Asks Camerarius to collect the remaining books from Brechtel's dispersed library and add any mathematics or chemical titles found, to be shipped via Georg Labenwolf.
Replies to Tycho's remarks on wasted clear skies and discusses the obstacles to astronomy from foul weather and academic neglect of the subject.
Reports that the Ptolemaic armillae have been entrusted to the mill craftsman to be fitted according to Tycho's specification, despite others' objections about water use.

documents.recipient_key: Rektor og professorer ved Københavns Universitet
documents.abstract: Thanks the university for his election as rector and declines the office, citing personal unfitness and pressing obligations that prevent him from discharging its duties.
Reports a prior letter of thanks for Tycho's treatise on the 1572 star, and describes discussions with Schissler and Gemperlin regarding the construction of a globe.
Urges Severinus to observe the current comet and to intercede with the King to prevent Tycho being called away before he completes his instrumental observations.
Notes Tycho's failure to write after Gemperlinus's return from Denmark, and reflects on the astrological prediction of danger to life Tycho had made for him.
Reports finding Maestlin's book on the 1577 comet in the Frankfurt catalogue and offers to forward it, discussing whether Tycho's own demonstration should supersede refutation of others.
Reports receiving German comet writings via Paul Hainzel, praises Maestlin's observations and demonstration above the rest, and discusses solar apogee, eccentricity, and the eighth sphere.
Excuses his infrequent letters due to difficulty in Latin, reports his household in good health, and notes the birth of a son in September 1577.
Writes briefly due to the courier's haste, reports inability to procure German comet writings, and comments on Danish language and the history of the Cimbri and Teutons.
Discusses arrangements regarding a horse offered by Master Franciscus and addresses an unnamed adversary's refusal of reconciliation, deferring judgment to the arriving Legate.
Invites Vedel and the Lord Legate to visit Hven, urging that Laurentius, Doctor Franciscus, Master Ezoccus, and the Royal Treasurer also accompany them.
Reminds Dançay of his promise to visit Hven, explains delays caused by travel between Zealand and Scania, and renews the invitation to come with friends.
Reports writing to Machabæus about horses and encloses letters of introduction to Camerarius, Hainzel, and Wolf in Nuremberg and Augsburg for Vedel's forthcoming journey.
Reports his health, criticises German astrologers for errors in predicting the recent eclipse, and urges Tycho's accurate observations to settle the disputed true motion of the Sun.
Accompanies two Danish students with a letter of introduction and notes that local astrologers erred in observing a recent eclipse, expecting more exact results from Tycho.
Apologises for the long silence, citing lack of letter-carriers, and introduces Paul Wittich, who has just delivered Hagecius's latest letter.
Thanks Scultetus for books received and critiques his treatise on the 1577 comet, disputing the parallax measurements as partly impossible and partly insufficiently observed.
Suspects earlier letters went astray, notes receipt of Hagecius's comet booklet brought by Bartholomaeus Scultetus, and prepares to offer the requested opinion on it.
Reports receiving Tycho's letter, regrets his own was not delivered, and defends Wittich, who conveyed Tycho's letter faithfully and invited Hagecius to join him on Hven.
Acknowledges receipt of Hagecius's letter via a Görlitz merchant, clears Wittich of suspicion, and sends a brief reply despite pressure of affairs and a royal summons.
Acknowledges Dançay's letter, urges him to endure court intrigues with composure, and conveys greetings from Erik Lange.

Disapproves of Brucaeus's neglect of mathematical studies, praises his plan to expound Proclus's Hypotheses, and requests a copy, while noting those Hypotheses rest on imperfect Ptolemaic foundations.
Declines the Holstein typographer Vedel proposed, reports engaging another printer and ordering type at the Frankfurt Fair to establish a press at Uraniborg.
Reports procuring books as requested, including Scaliger's work on the Gregorian calendar, and expresses relief at learning Tycho is still alive after rumours of his death.
Reports forwarding money to Tycho's printer via a carter and discusses solar and lunar motion, noting that Peurbach's calculations outperform Copernicus's in eclipse timings.
Acknowledges books received, declines the Wellerian ones, and argues that Lutheran theologians had no grounds to incite popular unrest over the Gregorian calendar reform.
Reports the Frankfurt bookseller brought none of the requested books, provides information on printing types available from Myliander, and notes Clavius's Gnomonice was sold to Rantzau.
Requests the return of a compass given to Tycho for repair, or if unavailable, asks that two new compasses of the same quality be made.
Sends paper and printing type obtained from Wittenberg, giving prices and delivery details, and notes the carter will bring remaining type once cast.
Reports the recent visit of Gerhard Rantzau to Uraniborg, praises his talents and character, and describes showing him the astronomical instruments and the new printing house.
Reports sending the type and books, and remonstrates against Tycho permitting a commonplace almanac with weather predictions to be published at his press.
Reports that Landgrave Wilhelm IV received Tycho's letter and comet treatise with great pleasure, that the Prince will write separately, and begins his own response on astronomical matters.
Rebukes Tycho for neglecting the Kullen beacon, citing sailors' complaints and noting that royal letters of command to the toll-officers have not been carried into effect.
Acknowledges receipt of payment, questions whether Tycho still intends to publish a calendar, and expresses skepticism that astrological prediction can be made reliable.
Thanks Hagecius for the kindness shown to his brother Steno Brahe during the latter's embassy to the Emperor, and pledges to repay the favour.
Reports improvements to the Kassel instruments following Paul Wittich's instruction, now achieving quarter-minute precision, and describes a new horizontal quadrant and sextant.
Reports the dismissal of a servant who committed theft and fornication with a maidservant, and asks Vedel's assistance in the resulting domestic matter.
Sends greetings via a chance messenger — a servant of the Navarrese ambassador passing through Prague — and notes the difficulty of correspondence across such distance.
Describes Uraniborg and its facilities, reports progress on astronomical and chemical works, and petitions the Emperor for an imperial printing privilege to protect publication.
Replies to his aunt's enquiry about a builder named Master Hans, who is expected within days, promising to relay her requirements when he arrives.
Responds to a copy of Wilhelm's letter to Heinrich Rantzau, expressing delight that the Landgrave continues to pursue astronomical studies at a mature age.
Reports hearing a (false) rumour of Tycho's death, announces the purchase of Clavius's Gnomonice and Magini's Tables with Ephemerides on his behalf, and asks confirmation.
Excuses a delayed reply by winter ice blocking the island, and reports having already sent Wilhelm IV a compendious description of the comet observations.

documents.recipient_key: [Imperial printing privilege in favour of Tycho Brahe]
documents.abstract: Grants Tycho Brahe a ten-year imperial printing privilege, prohibiting all printers and booksellers from reproducing his mathematical works without authorisation.
Thanks Tycho for the comet observations and reports that the Kassel mathematician's observations agree closely with Tycho's after equation of times and longitudes.
Explains the mutual delay: Tycho's August letter arrived only in March, and Hagecius's lucubrations were returned from Frankfurt after the Navarrese ambassador changed his route.
Acknowledges simultaneous receipt of two letters, Hagecius's revised Dialexis, and the Imperial printing privilege, and discusses the contents of these items.
Reminds Young of his promise to visit Uraniborg and invites him to come the following day, noting that Erik Lange and Falk Gøye also await his arrival.
Follows up on his unanswered April letter, notes that comet and nova-near-Cassiopeia observations agree closely, and requests Tycho's judgment on the Kassel observations.
Asks Tycho to confirm receipt of earlier letters and Werner's book, and notes that Jacobus Curtius, Vice-Chancellor of the Empire, eagerly awaits Tycho's first publication.
Asks why Tycho has not replied to letters sent via the Frankfurt fair and conveys the Landgrave's repeated inquiries about the delayed answer.
Reminds Tycho of two unanswered letters, renewing the request to send his observations of the fixed stars for comparison with Kassel's own.
Apologizes for the long delay in replying, attributing it to distance and infrequent mail opportunities, and begins addressing the Landgrave's astronomical inquiries.
Praises the correspondence between Tycho and the Landgrave as beneficial to astronomy and congratulates the age for producing princes devoted to the study of the science.
Acknowledges Rothmann's April letter with its recondite astronomical discussions, explains the delay in replying, and reports having communicated celestial observations to the Landgrave.
Returns Hagecius's manuscript on the new star and comets via the Frankfurt fair and advises him to revise his treatment of the 1577 comet before publishing.
Introduces a young scholar visiting Tycho, urges completion of the star catalogue's longitudes and latitudes, and endorses Tycho's dissent from prior authorities if experience warrants it.
Intercedes for his former bailiff Christoffer Pepler, seeking recovery of debts withheld by Nordfjord peasants and reimbursement for buildings erected on a waste plot.
Reports that a messenger returned from Frankfurt with no letters, explaining that the Landgrave had been occupied with a wedding and has promised a reply by courier shortly.
Thanks Tycho for his observations and reports close agreement with Kassel's in distances and declinations to fractions of a minute, though a five-minute discrepancy in longitudes remains.
Requests the almanacs for 1588 that Tycho had promised, asking him to send them by the current messenger if ready or complete them as soon as possible.
Apologizes for the delayed reply, acknowledges Tycho's parallax argument for the comet, but reports his own observations cannot detect parallax, engaging Copernican hypotheses on the point.
Apologizes for summer silence, explaining he awaited the Landgrave's reply before forwarding copies of their astronomical correspondence, which he now encloses.
Thanks Tycho for copies of the Hven–Kassel correspondence and engages the evidence for stellar latitude changes linked to variation in the obliquity of the ecliptic.
Corrects a misquotation in his previous letter: the writers on optics place the dense atmosphere's upper limit not at one terrestrial semidiameter but at a much smaller fraction.
Addresses the question, forwarded from Duke Ulrich of Mecklenburg, of whether Tobias Möller's or Andreas Rosa's assignment of planetary rulers for 1588 is correct.
Confirms Hagecius's manuscript was sent to Frankfurt, advises him to revise his treatment of the 1577 comet, and sends the second volume of his own work on it.
Introduces a Brandenburg knight, Haken, who wishes to visit, and mentions composing a panegyric of the Danish king to be sent in June.
Excuses a delayed reply on grounds of illness and pressing occupations, and reports ongoing Venus observations intended to settle a five-minute longitude discrepancy between their star positions.
Reports that fifty-five reams of printing paper, delayed by mould-adaptation, have been forwarded via Master Peter the clockmaker as a gift.
Explains a delayed reply by missed courier opportunities and ongoing Venus observations, which he intends to compare with prior morning observations before writing more fully.
Notes the second book of *De mundi aetherei* was sent in May, and urges a frank written opinion of its contents before winter cuts off correspondence.

Asks for written judgment on the recently sent second book on aethereal phenomena, and asserts that his extensive dissent from Scultetus's views reflects philosophical liberty, not personal antagonism.
Excuses a late reply and, having already sent the second book of *De mundi aetherei* via Gellius Sascerides, asks for Rothmann's frank opinion of its contents.
Thanks Rantzau for procuring printing paper and for the chapel engraving honouring the late King, and sends the promised horizontal sundial, delayed because Gerhard Rantzau departed without visiting.
Opens a correspondence via Rantzau's introduction and undertakes to address Peucer's doubts about the diagram of Tycho's new world-system hypothesis conveyed through Rantzau.
Reports forwarding a letter to Bording and the type-founder's refusal to cross to Denmark, and praises the first part of the comet-of-1577 book.
Acknowledges both recent letters and the second tome of *De mundi aetherei*, then argues persistently that the celestial matter is elemental air and not aether.
Reports two earlier letters apparently lost, confirms receipt of the book in late July with expressions of delight, and regrets that advancing age limits fuller engagement.
Forgives a summer silence and responds to Brucaeus's comments on the second *Aetherial Phenomena* book, welcoming his approval of the earlier sections and of the new hypothesis.
Confirms receipt of the sundial, letters, and celestial-hypothesis instrument, then gives instructions for setting the sundial's meridian line by compass and solar observations.
Questions whether Brucaeus, despite his stated practice of pressing hard on disputed points before assenting, truly avoids prejudice in weighing opinions, citing evidence from earlier conversations.

Resumes the astronomical correspondence despite receiving no reply, understanding that preparations for a daughter's marriage occupied Wilhelm, and noting that Rothmann had written on the Landgrave's behalf.
Excuses a delayed reply to Rothmann's most recent letter and engages with his persistent argument that the celestial matter is elemental air, finding his evasions unconvincing.
Uses Tage Krabbe's departure for Prague as a courier opportunity to press Hagecius once more for a still-awaited reply and further conference.
Objects that Tycho's reply lacked expected candour and misread his words, and defends his stated practice of pressing hard on disputed points before assenting.
Acknowledges receipt of Tycho's letter and book via William Stuart, thanks him for the gift, and expresses eagerness for the friendship Liddel had proposed.
Reports that a previous letter and Werner's book, sent via Mylius at Görlitz, failed to reach Tycho, and explains the transmission arrangements made.
Acknowledges Tycho's letter and the Tycho–Landgrave Wilhelm comparative observations, delayed four months in transit, and replies via Duke John of Holstein as a courier.
Reports missing Tycho's courier to the Emperor and failing to obtain the book by Io. Francus from the Frankfurt fair booksellers for dispatch.
Refers to a previous hurried reply on Tycho's question, then reports the universal joy and prayer in Scotland for King James to find a consort.
Resumes discussion of Tycho's celestial hypothesis, arguing that Mars at acronychal position nearer than the Sun is an absurdity, and proposes alternative geometric solutions.
Instructs Rothmann to write to Tycho via Nicodemus Frischlin, travelling to Denmark, asking what Tycho has in hand and when his earlier work will appear.
Reports that no reply from Tycho arrived at the Frankfurt fair, explains the Landgrave's pressing concern, and notes Frischlin has arrived with a letter from the Prince.
Defends his previous letter against Tycho's misreading, denying he detracted from Scripture's authority, and cites Augustine as a precedent for speaking freely on sacred texts.
Orders Tycho to maintain the beacon on Kullen more diligently, as seafarers have been complaining about its upkeep.
Directs Tycho to account before the Council of the Regency for wax salvaged from a 1587 English shipwreck off Anholt, which the crown claims as wreck.
Sends via William Stuart an apologetic reply to Craig's three summer letters, defending the supralunary position of comets and his innovation in celestial hypotheses.
Acknowledges four letters from Hagecius received over the summer, detailing each one's dispatch and arrival dates and noting the constant delays in transmission.
Requests Vedel's overdue draft of the Danish Privilege for the first volume now at press, and asks help finding a papermaker for the newly ready mill.
Clarifies that his previous letter accused Rothmann not of impiety but only of misapplying Moses's description of the Moon as 'lesser light' to questions of physical magnitude.
Reports approaching the royal legate Vinshemius for a letter from Tycho but finding none, and protests that he has always answered Tycho's letters.
Postpones his visit to Copenhagen and asks Madsen to prevent any communication to the Lord Chancellor in Gellius's name regarding his not-yet-received master's degree.
Explains the delay in replying: Bongars, a French envoy who delivered Peucer's second letter in Copenhagen, departed for Germany before Tycho could send a reply.
Asks Rantzau to remind Tycho that letters sent the previous September — one from the Landgrave and two from Rothmann on astronomical matters — still await a reply.
Reassures Hagecius that his earlier letters arrived, explains the missed chance to write via Winshemius, and notes fewer visits to court since King Frederick's death.
Sends a letter via the approaching Frankfurt fair, with little new substance to report but unwilling to let the occasion pass without writing.
Chides Rothmann for slow replies and reports that printing of his first volume is nearly finished, with the third and final part now in press.
Reports hearing from Fuller about Tycho's reception and his reply to Craig's first letter, and declares willingness to yield to Tycho's demonstrations if they prove sound.
Acknowledges Tycho's work in astronomy and the construction of Uraniborg under the late King Frederick's patronage; the letter's rubric identifies it as concerning Tycho's children.
Reports a new, pale comet now visible and sends observations, citing the Landgrave's known interest in such phenomena from the comet of five years before.
Apologizes for delay, reports the inquiry into the Stures' arms via his sister Sophia and Lady Gørvel still unsatisfied, and promises to write when resolved.
Excuses his delayed reply by describing two years of severe illness — gout and kidney stones — which so weakened him that he could barely trace a letter.
Acknowledges receipt of three letters including the Apologia, promises a full reply via courier Curtius, and requests specimen models of the sextant and armillae.
Explains his silence by Rothmann's illness and his own advancing age, lamenting that mathematical studies he once pursued eagerly are now barely comprehensible to him.
Praises Tycho's letter for its warm recollection of their friendship and learned astronomical disquisition, which he found entirely welcome rather than over-long.
Thanks Tycho for his letter, declares long-standing admiration for his writings, and describes an earnest desire to visit in person, prevented only by Imperial duty.
Demands repayment of a 1,000-daler loan already twice overdue and orders payment at the current Diet in Kolding without further delay.
Thanks Kurz for procuring the Imperial Privilege on his behalf and for writing so luminous a reply despite heavy duties of public administration.
Reports receipt of the new Imperial Privilege via Prague courier, thanks Hagecius for moving Curtius to obtain it, and notes a lost transcript of the Gallican privilege.
Grants a further extension on Tycho's 1,000-daler debt to fourteen days after Michaelmas while insisting on payment by that date without further delay or neglect.
Thanks Tycho for sending his book via a Danish student, notes the rarity of Danish publications in Italy, and welcomes the ensuing opportunity for scholarly exchange.
Notes Magini's approval of his book, discusses his promise to amend planetary tables, and cites a half-degree tabular error in the Sun at the vernal equinox.
Reports Rothmann's arrival at Uraniborg with Wilhelm's letter and acknowledges the reasons given for the long interruption in correspondence.
Chides Vedel for long silence, reports the press stands idle for lack of paper, and asks help finding a skilled papermaker for the new Uraniborg mill.
Welcomes news that the second book of the Phaenomenon did not displease Camerarius and that it has been forwarded to Vincenzo Pinelli at Padua.
Asks Young to convey thanks for the royal visit to Uraniborg and to solicit a privilege for the typographical labors, while chiding him for long silence.
Acknowledges Savile's letter forwarded via Winsheim, welcomes the correspondence of learned men from across Europe, and notes that English visitors have previously come to Uraniborg.
Reports a plan to have the latitudes and longitudes of principal European places determined by dispatching instruments and observers, with a man to be sent shortly.
Acknowledges Magini's receipt of the second book of De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis through Gellius Sascerides and notes the letter from Bologna, received 24 November.
Presses Rantzau for help procuring a papermaker needed to resume printing at Uraniborg, naming specifically a Caspar who may be working at Rantzau's mill.
Reports that printing is stalled because the papermaker sent to Germany has absconded, leaving the Uraniborg mill idle and the first volume delayed.
Instructs Gellius and Magini on conducting solar, stellar, and lunar observations at Padua to determine the meridian difference with Uraniborg and to fix principles of atmospheric refraction.
Acknowledges Hagecius's acceptance of Tycho's replies to his astronomical objections and praises his candor in conceding rather than defending untenable positions.
Asks Tycho to write about conditions in Denmark and to share fixed-star observations for comparison with Kassel's, and mentions a reported unusual animal.
Acknowledges Rothmann's report of prolonged illness and the sketch of Tycho's observatory, wishes him recovery, and cautions that the ailments should not be self-inflicted by excess.
Defends himself against Wilhelm's complaint of sparse correspondence by noting that earlier letters with comet observations were apparently never received, as Rothmann was also unaware of them.
Welcomes news that the first volume of De recentioribus coeli Phaenomenis is in press, noting particular interest in the fixed-star content, and inquires about Rothmann's welfare.
Asks the Rector to convene Niels Krag and Niels Colding before colleagues to give sworn attestation before Tycho's bailiff regarding events witnessed on Tycho's behalf.
Reports that the requested Padua observations of the pole and stellar meridian altitudes remain unconducted due to unsuitable conditions, and announces a dedicated work shortly to be sent.
Concedes complete defeat in the astronomical disputation with Tycho, reports distributing copies of Tycho's portrait among friends including Curtius who forwarded one to Bavaria.
Orders Tycho to repair the Chapel of the Three Holy Kings at Roskilde Cathedral before winter, invoking obligations in his letter of enfeoffment.
Requests the elk Tycho promised, wanting it as a companion for his deer-park elk, and offers Zapfenburger wine in return.
Explains the three-and-a-half-month delay in receiving Wilhelm's May letter, then discusses the first volume of *De Recentioribus coeli Phaenomenis* and its treatment of the stellar restoration.
Reports that the promised elk broke its leg and died before it could be sent, and notes that a prior letter explaining this was dispatched via Henrik Ramel.
Asks Metellus to compose a poem to accompany Tycho's portrait in his forthcoming works, thanking him for epigrams inscribed on Hven's gate during a previous visit.
Challenges Craig for falling silent in their ongoing dispute, arguing that acknowledging errors is praiseworthy and urging him either to concede or to continue the debate.
Announces the discovery of a quick method for extracting square roots of large numbers after years of effort, and previews the result for Tycho before wider publication.
Reports that elk are on order from Norway but winter has delayed shipping, promises to inform Wilhelm when animals are ready for collection in spring, and mentions writing to Rothmann.
Reproaches Rothmann for nearly eighteen months of silence since his visit to Hven, and reports learning through Rothmann's brother Johannes that he had been detained by illness.
Introduces himself formally to Moritz, recalling a brief meeting at Kassel when Moritz was young and noting Rothmann's report that Tycho's name is already known to him.
Sends the first printed gathering of his forthcoming works with its contents table, and asks Scultetus to show it to local booksellers and negotiate terms for copies.
Requests a measure of *smerle* clay from Hven for her father Duke Ulrich of Mecklenburg, and asks for a further supply of burnt antimony.
Responds to Blotius's letter, acknowledging that their Swiss acquaintance of more than twenty-two years earlier had entirely slipped from memory, and welcomes renewed contact.
Reproves Peter Young for not answering two or three previous letters, arguing that frequent shipping between Scotland and Denmark makes such prolonged silence inexcusable.

Sends the first printed gathering of the *Progymnasmata* with six extra copies for distribution, explaining that Curtius persuaded him to publish a forerunner volume of his planned astronomical restoration.
Reports reading Tycho's *Apologia* and composing a reply to its first argument, which was delayed when the ship carrying it turned back upon learning the Danish king had departed.
Thanks Tycho for elk-procurement efforts, and reports that three of four elk recently obtained from Sweden have died, possibly from eating rotten acorns after an unusually heavy mast year.
Demurs at Tycho's high praise of his poetic abilities, but nonetheless sends a commendatory poem for the forthcoming *Opera Astronomica* as requested.
Thanks Brahe for his November letter and the engraved portrait attached, recalling the friendship formed during his recent journey through Denmark.
Asks why the promised Norwegian elk have not been delivered, noting his April courier went unanswered and that his existing Swedish elk have all died.
Lists errata in the controversy copy sent to Brahe and announces he will make his full reply, undeterred by Brahe's disciples or teachers.
Explains the delay in replying to Maitland's letter, citing the unexpected impediment to his planned messengers, and now writes via passing merchants.
Explains the delay in delivering the promised Norwegian elk, reporting that his kinsman Axel Gyldenstierne found no skipper willing to transport them safely from Norway.
Thanks Moritz for composing a commendatory poem for the astronomical works and notes that the verses will stand as a lasting token of his favour.
Reports receiving no letter from Hagecius all summer and attributes the silence to courier faithlessness rather than any failure on Hagecius's part.
Complains of Young's long silence despite several letters and renews a request to obtain a poem from the King of Scots through Young's good offices.
Reports finding no printer's assistant via Myliander and questions how Craig can refute the parallax evidence placing the recent comet in the supralunary region.
Forwards a complaint from Rasmus Pedersen of Gunderslevmagle, who alleges Brahe has denied him his leased farm and unlawfully imprisoned his brother and servant.
Explains his long silence by recounting months of serious illness: recurring stomach pain followed by jaundice and a continuous fever lasting through the summer.
Reports to Moritz that the Norwegian elk repeatedly promised to his late father Wilhelm could not be delivered alive despite repeated efforts.
Reports Galileo's new mathematics chair at Padua, Maginus's Tabula Tetragonica under Tycho's patronage, and a Venetian plan to dispatch a mathematician to Egypt on Tycho's behalf.
Asks Rantzau to assist with forwarding perspective drawings sent by his former architect, now supervising construction of Varberg castle in Halland.
Thanks Kurz for securing the Imperial privilege for his astronomical works and recalls Kurz's earlier expressions of goodwill and favour toward the mathematical arts.
Acknowledges Hagecius's December letter describing his serious illnesses, expresses sympathy, and advises against strong purging medicines in favour of gentle remedies suited to old age.
Protests Young's continuing silence and asks whether previous letters and an elegiac epistle intended for the Scottish King arrived safely.
Apologizes for prolonged silence, choosing confession over excuses, and assures Brahe his goodwill remains unchanged, with the ambassadors offered as pledges of his constancy.
Accepts Young's apology for a long epistolary silence and thanks him for procuring items as requested, with news passed through the returning lord ambassadors.
Apologizes for a year of epistolary silence, attributing it to the burdens of office, poor health, and failing memory in his sixty-eighth year.
Expresses relief at Hagecius's survival, questions whether his earlier letter and two copies of the *Progymnasmata Astronomica* were received.
Thanks Tycho for favorable mention in a letter to Young, pledges devotion, and asks that any remaining offence from his brother be forgiven.
Grants Tycho a royal privilege protecting the forthcoming *Progymnasmata Astronomica* against unauthorized reprinting.
Seeks to renew friendship after the cooling caused by a previous disputation, crediting Master Junius's mediation with reopening contact.
Orders reconsideration of Christoffer Pepeler's imprisonment on Hven, following his wife's petition that he was detained despite posting bail after his goods were seized.
Thanks Craig for his letters, explains a missed meeting with Junius at Helsingør, and briefly addresses the dispute over comets.
Declares the sale of his half-share of Knudstrup to his brother Steen Brahe, reserving the right to retain the style 'of Knudstrup' for life.
Rebukes Tycho for failing to repair the Chapel of the Three Holy Kings at Roskilde Cathedral and demands completion before Christmas.
Explains his long absence by severe arthritis and nephritic pain, reports a partial recovery, and mentions searching Frankfurt catalogues.
Apologizes for six months of silence due to remote location, reporting a previous letter sent via a Marburg messenger accompanying a paper-maker for Tycho's mill.
Authorizes replacing the Roskilde chapel vaulting with beams and orders the renovation of the Chapel of the Three Holy Kings completed without delay.

documents.sender_key: Rektor og professorerne ved Københavns Universitet
documents.abstract: Presents a complaint from their miller Lauge against Tycho's servant Peder over a mill dispute, asking Tycho to punish his man or allow legal proceedings.

documents.recipient_key: Rektor og professorerne ved Københavns Universitet
documents.abstract: Responds to the mill complaint by reporting that the opposing party refused a hearing and the offered transcript of five letters, leaving no further obligation.

documents.recipient_key: Rektor og professorerne ved Københavns Universitet
documents.abstract: Defends his position in the mill dispute, reporting that the opposing party refused to acknowledge the reading of five letters or accept the offered transcript.
Acknowledges Rothmann's long-awaited letter, condoles with him over prolonged illness from Tartareous salts, and resumes their suspended astronomical correspondence.
Expresses joy at receiving Hagecius's letter after nearly three years of silence, having feared that advancing age and illness had proved fatal.
Replies to two letters, notes that an expected visitor has not arrived, and complains that the globe-maker Sphaeropaeus has sent neither correspondence nor globes, apparently gripped by avarice.
Affirms the family bond with Tycho, professes sincere regard and admiration for his learning, and promises faithful service in whatever matter Tycho may require.
Explains that admiration for Tycho long deterred him from writing to so eminent a man, but a forwarded letter from Rantzau has now prompted him to make contact.
Asks Rosenkrantz to prevent a defendant from fleeing to court, where Tycho is pressing a legal suit requiring testimony in defence of his reputation.
Thanks Aslaksen for Pitiscus's book on triangles, praises it, and invites Pitiscus to correspond, expressing a wish that more clergymen possessed skill in geometry.
Responds to news that Pontanus is now in England, commends his literary studies there, and urges him to secure an English publication privilege before Pentecost.
Presses the rector of the University of Copenhagen for a definitive written reply from the consistory on two pending matters, having received only vague assurances thus far.
Accepts the rector's refusal to show the unsealed statement, but requests that all consistory acts relating to his case be subscribed on each page, sealed, and retained until needed.
Reports that Tycho's letters were safely delivered and presents a candidate to manage the fief and command of Nordfjord on Tycho's behalf.
Argues that it falls to the new chancellor to support astronomy and the liberal disciplines, citing Manilius on the art's glory for kingdoms and kings.
Corrects the claim that he left Denmark merely because of revenue losses, arguing that all his revenues were withdrawn and that his emigration had deeper causes.
Reports the king's refusal of both Tycho's requests: no treasury funds for the upkeep of astronomical instruments, and no extension of the Norwegian benefice.

Thanks Rantzau for forwarding dispatches and promises regarding correction of the Spanish patent, and reports receiving a request from Archbishop Ernst of Cologne for astronomical and astrological communication.
Sends theses he helped arrange for publication, notes having forwarded Tycho's first letter-volume to Élie, and recalls being a guest of Tycho's in 1584.
Notes that several letters, some for Rantzau's eyes only, have gone unanswered, and urges a reply, assuring him the matter discussed is being actively pursued.
Certifies that Longomontanus served faithfully for nearly eight years in astronomical work, conducted himself virtuously, and is released at his own request with a commendation to all.
Congratulates Rostock on Tycho's arrival, quotes Cicero on the disgrace of expelling a great man from his homeland, and prays for Tycho's flourishing in the city.
Explains the delay in replying due to his departure from Denmark, thanks Moritz for investigating Erik Lange's financial affairs and debts, and reports currently tarrying at Rostock.
Recounts twenty-two years of astronomical work on Hven at Frederick II's encouragement and justifies his departure, having had no opportunity for a royal audience beforehand.
Thanks the Duke for his past visit to Hven, explains his departure from Denmark for unstated weighty reasons, and reports current residence in Rostock.
Acknowledges Tycho's departure from Denmark, grieves the loss to astronomy, and promises to present his letter to the Duke and procure a letter of recommendation.
Acknowledges displeasure at Tycho's changed circumstances, recalls seeing the instruments on Hven, and expresses regret that the astronomical work may not be brought to completion.
Intercedes with King Christian IV on Tycho's behalf, arguing that his departure risks leaving his astronomical works unfinished, and recommends him to royal favour.
Apologizes for failing to write earlier amid departure preparations and explains his decision to remain at Rostock to give his countrymen time to reconsider.
Thanks Rantzau for estates offered and requests a location near a large town where a printing-house, engravers, and instrument-makers are available to complete his books.
Acknowledges Tycho's letter from Rostock summarising his loss of astronomical stipend, lack of means to continue independently, and assertion that his departure was blameless.
Reports withdrawal from plague-struck Rostock to Holstein at Rantzau's invitation, where several castles have been placed at his disposal.
Laments the ill-will and avarice of those who misled the young King against him, driving him from Denmark; text is heavily fragmentary.
Corrects an earlier error in Jupiter observations, supplying revised distances from Aldebaran and the shoulder of Orion, and notes dissatisfaction with his sextant's graduated scale.
Introduces himself to Tycho, sends the Prodromus dissertationum cosmographicarum, and requests Tycho's judgment on the work, citing Maestlin's prior approval.
Apologizes for delayed reply due to wedding festivities and expresses grief not for Tycho personally but for the fatherland that has wronged him.
Explains that his departure from Denmark was prompted by pressing reasons and not intended as a slight to the King, who may have been misled by ill-wishers.
Reports meeting the Lord Administrator and his consort at Bramstedt and departing with his household for Hamburg for Christmas.
Relays that Scaliger has incorporated Tycho's vernal and autumnal observations into his own work and suggests Holland would suit Tycho better than Germany.
Thanks Hagecius for arranging to send a defamatory pamphlet and declines to reply to its author, deeming him unworthy of refutation.
Addresses Rudolf II invoking the Imperial tradition of astronomical patronage and solicits the Emperor's clement reception of his petition.
Reports learning from Matthew Roydon that Tycho has moved to Germany, expresses relief at sparing a journey to Denmark, and hopes Tycho may settle in Hesse.
Accepts the excuses of Rosenkrantz and Cragius for not visiting, urges Holger to free himself from court obligations and return to virtue and learning.
Asks the Danish Steward and Chancellor to support Tycho Brahe with the king, noting the Elector has written separately to the royal family on Tycho's behalf.
Intercedes on Tycho Brahe's behalf with Christian IV, noting the Elector knows only Tycho's own account and expects the king to act fairly regardless.
Exchanges greetings and inquires after the king's health, reporting that the Electress herself has been suffering from a cough for several days.
Thanks Christian IV for his father Frederick II's patronage of astronomy and complains that hidden enemies have maliciously obstructed him without cause.
Asks Rosenkrantz for the name, address, and preferred language of an Austrian baron introduced by Erik Lange, in order to solicit testimony about the plagiarist Ursus.
Sends her servant Johann Müller to study mathematics and spagyric preparation of medicaments under Tycho, requesting compliance with the terms previously promised.
Rebukes Vedel for adopting a judge's tone and for failing to keep a promised journey, addressing also some matters concerning Lange and English letters.
Explains a delayed reply by three months of illness, thanks Tycho for his letter and the items enclosed, and reports recovering health.
Reports completing business with Johann Bokel, the Duke of Brunswick's agreement with Tycho's view, and the absence of news about the Queen's arrival in Hamburg.
Introduces himself to Scaliger via the bearer Frans Tengnagel, expresses long-held admiration, and praises the newly received *De Temporum Emendatione*.
Thanks Longomontanus for his concern, asks about Wittich's manuscripts and their price at Wittich's sister's house, and mentions Ursus's slanderous writing against Tycho's honour.
Asks Winshemius to press Bökel to deliver books already paid for by Holger Rosenkrantz, threatening legal action if Bökel refuses to honour his promises.
Asks Bording to present a personal letter to Duke Ulrich and to interpret it charitably if overly frank, urging complete secrecy about its contents.
Warmly acknowledges two letters from Rosenkrantz expressing deep affection, though noting they were tinged with bitterness by some unhappy news they also conveyed.
Formally acknowledges requesting a 100-thaler advance from the Mecklenburg treasury, to be deducted from the 600 thalers owed to Tycho when the revenue falls due.
Describes how a kinsman at the Imperial court shared Ursus's attacking pamphlet, which was briefly lost through a friend's carelessness before being recovered.
Acknowledges Kepler's letter and praises the *Prodromus Dissertationum Cosmographicarum*, admiring its wit and the ingenious speculation binding planetary distances to the regular solids.
Presses Vedel to respond about provisions to be procured for Tycho's use and to enlist friends and kinsmen in securing them.
Recalls a ten-year-old promise by Maestlin to read and comment on Tycho's 1577 comet book, and reproaches him for never writing.
Relays news of Erik Sparre's promises at Rostock, reports uncertainty about the Kolding assembly, and comments on Rantzau's role.
Sends a promised Propempticon poem for Tycho's Urania, confirms dispatch of the testimony on the Liddelian plagiarism, and announces his doctoral promotion at Wittenberg.
Thanks Valkendorf for the support he gives Tycho's bailiff on Hven in managing disobedient peasants and settling their claims.
Urges Tycho to come to Prague without delay, reporting that Vice-Chancellor Coraduz has commended him favourably to the Emperor.
Thanks Grynaeus for his sympathetic letter regarding the envy and malevolence of certain men that drove Tycho from Denmark.
Shares his kinsman's intelligence about Ursus and the Emperor's expectation of Tycho, and reports speaking with the Lord of Brunswick on Tycho's behalf.
Reports two printing errors in the Mechanica — a missing 'I' before 'Curtio' and 'GENEROSE' printed for 'INGENIOSE' — and asks Rosenkrantz to correct them.
Expresses keen pleasure at Brahe's work samples and Rantzau's recommendation, and promises to continue cherishing Brahe as worthy of Denmark and Germany.
Acknowledges Tycho's gift of books and the report of his affairs brought by the bearer, and pledges continued commendation to the Emperor.
Commends to the Emperor Tycho Brahe's resolve to leave Denmark and settle in Germany under imperial protection, praising his learning and renown.
Asks the imperial secretary to ensure Tycho receives a prompt decision on his petition, calling him the sole restorer of astronomy.
Responds to Tycho's letter, returns greetings to Monau and the Bucretius brothers, and addresses the request for copies of Melanchthon letters.
Forwards copies of letters from a Magdeburg friend reporting the Emperor's disposition toward Tycho, and notes he must reply to Eske Bille.
Reports in detail his embassy to Elector Ernst of Cologne at Aachen and Liège, delivering Tycho's letters and receiving the Elector's warm patronage promises.
Expresses relief at finally learning Tycho's whereabouts after his departure from Denmark, and writes now that his location at Wandsbek is known.
Reports conversations about the causes of Tycho's departure from Denmark, defending the fatherland against those who condemn it for losing him.
Reports receiving Holger's delayed letter, notes the Brandenburg electoral letters were not presented to the King, and alludes to collusion between the two Chancellors.
Reports that Tycho left Denmark voluntarily when his astronomical work could no longer be valued, and that Ulrich interceded with the Danish king on his behalf.
Reports Mule's return without the money owed; Eske failed to obtain two thousand joachims at Flensburg, and Accius defers payment citing his dead brother's debts.
Thanks Scaliger for his concern about affairs, for discussions of chronology and stellar reckoning, and for courteously receiving Tengnagel; declines to detail the reasons for his departure.
Urges Holger to reply to earlier letters without further delay and to dispatch the promised wagon from Aarhus to Lübeck, which is holding up the journey.
Clarifies that the promised wagon has not arrived in Lübeck, contradicting Holger's assumption, and repeats the request to send it without further delay.
Reports Winsheim's inquiry with Böckel about the late Pieremann's books: Böckel had sold them wholesale to Holger Rosenkrantz for 150 thalers and handed them over to Claus Mule.
Writes again through Frans Rantzau to press Holger once more about the promised wagon, which has still not arrived in Lübeck despite repeated requests.
Thanks Duke Ulrich for his gracious reply and for sending a letter of commendation to the Emperor, and acknowledges the Duke's favorable reception of the Mechanica.
Reports that the long-promised wagon has reached Oldesloe but the delay had forced him to buy a replacement at Hamburg for fifty joachimsthalers three days before.
Thanks Tycho for his letter, which Chytraeus regards as a singular honour, and praises Tycho's gracious acknowledgment of the University of Rostock's welcome.
Commends a former household student traveling to Italy and sends two bound books for the Grand Duke, seconding a recommendation already given by Heinrich Rantzau.
Reports that the Emperor desires Tycho's presence but has not settled a court residence due to the plague, and advises waiting for Rudolf's final arrangement.
Acknowledges, five years after receipt, Magini's Tabula Tetragonica (dedicated to him) and notes his approval while observing that the calculations are not fully worked through.
Forwards a note from Coraduz bearing the Emperor's resolution, received just before Hagecius's departure, and adds nothing further beyond this dispatch.
Reports his journey from Wandsbek toward Prague, with stops at Magdeburg and Dresden while awaiting the Emperor's reply, and announces his son Tycho's departure.
Reports receiving Krag's October letter and wonders why Holger retained earlier letters meant for Krag, urging Krag to answer promptly and explain what was done with those letters.
Recounts the journey from Wandsbek toward Prague, halted at Dresden when plague in Bohemia worsened and the Emperor withdrew, having been summoned through Coraduz and Hagecius.
Reports a Hamburg printer's corruption of the lunar-motion gatherings, plans to reprint them correctly at Wittenberg, and thanks Longomontanus for staying with his household at Wandsbek.
Reports wintering at Wittenberg because epidemic plague prevents travel to Bohemia, notes the Emperor is similarly displaced, and asks Rosenkrantz for news from Denmark.
Thanks Tycho for two volumes sent as a gift, praises the work, and expresses willingness to receive the remaining volumes when opportunity allows.
Informs Meier that his eldest daughter has borrowed two hundred thalers against interest, acknowledges the bond given in return, and reports delays in receiving funds from Denmark.
A formal quittance acknowledging receipt of two hundred reichsthaler in advance interest from rent-master Andreas Meyer, signed and sealed at Wittenberg.
Urges Longomontanus to travel to Wittenberg, offers travel funds, and proposes either the Imperial Mathematician post at Prague or an academic position at Wittenberg.
Transmits the Emperor's command summoning Tycho immediately to Prague and expresses personal eagerness to meet him in person.
Laments the moral corruption and religious disorder of the age, citing Virgil on irreversible decline, before the text breaks off; little substantive content beyond this preserved.
Explains the ten-month delay receiving Tycho's reply via Maestlin, acknowledges most excerpted words in his Ursus letters as his own, but sees no proven crime in their publication.
Reports the imperial summons to Prague via Coraduz, explains delay due to deep snow and horses sold at Leipzig, and plans to depart within fourteen days.
Thanks Winsheim for letters, apologizes for delayed replies, and confirms his son has already informed him of the imperial summons to Prague via Coraduz.
Advises Tycho to surrender Hven to the King tactfully by letter, keeping his instruments, and not to seek restitution of expenses; text is heavily lacunose throughout.
Reports John Craig's disparagement of Tycho as arrogant, his grievance over Tycho's complaint to the King of Scotland, and his dismissal of Tycho's published letters against him.
Encourages Longomontanus's refutation of the Scottish Capnurania and directs him to the second book on the 1577 comet, particularly the Noltius section, for parallax arguments.
Thanks Scaliger for two books sent as gifts and for excerpting, in his own hand, the key passages from Hipparchus and Ptolemy on the fixed stars.
Reports non-receipt of earlier letters and no contact with Tengnagel, asks Tycho to repeat what was entrusted, and directs future correspondence via a Prague bookseller.
Acknowledges Rosenkrantz's letter on the vernal equinox and relays Vice-Chancellor Coraduz’s messages conveying the Emperor’s favour and the summons to Prague.
Congratulates Tycho on his imperial summons to Prague, expresses confidence the Emperor will retain him there, and offers assistance with Tycho's studies.
Reports Emperor Rudolf II's generous reception at Prague, his lodging in the Curtius house, and his preference to seek a more secluded residence outside the city.
Reports his establishment at Benátky castle under imperial patronage and plans to pursue astronomical and alchemical work there, with instruments being transferred from Magdeburg.
Recounts the journey from Wittenberg to Bohemia, detailing delays caused by a daughter's illness, the completion of a book for the Emperor, and hospitality received en route.
Acknowledges receipt of Tycho's lunar eclipse calculation, congratulates him on imperial patronage, and discusses whether the star of Mercury can eclipse Venus.
Narrates the circumstances of his departure from Denmark, recounting his warning to the King's Chancellor about the threatened fate of his observatory at Uraniborg.
Informs Sophie Brahe that 300 dalers he had ready were paid out elsewhere due to her messenger's delay, and arranges for payment through Sten Maltesen instead.
Asks Longomontanus to accompany his son and Mule to Denmark to retrieve remaining instruments, reporting that imperial secretary Barvitius has written to Henrik Ramel to facilitate the transfer.
Thanks Mette Mule for her letter received at Wittenberg, apologises for the delay in reply, and reports that brother Tyge and Claus Mule are travelling to Denmark.
Refers Cramer to an enclosed copy of his letter to Holger Rosenkrantz for news of his situation, requesting confidentiality, and hints at a separate matter personally concerning Cramer.
Informs the Hamburg city council of his imperial summons and generous reception at Rudolf II's court, noting the Emperor's awareness of instruments and goods left behind in Denmark.
Reports that imperial letters on Tycho's behalf have not yet been presented to Hamburg's Senate due to his people's carelessness, and promises to promote the matter once they are read.
Reports accompanying her son Tage on his journey, describing travel through Haderslev and Lindved to Breitenburg, where Gert Rantzau is helping arrange his onward passage to Basel.
Expresses gladness at hearing of Tycho's favourable terms with the Emperor and pledges to help prevent any interference with the retrieval of his instruments if it arises.
Acknowledges Tycho's good standing with the Emperor (noted at the Herredag assembly), discusses 50 thaler owed to Longomontanus, and advises routing the instruments via Lübeck.
Reports Tengnagel's Carnival visit delivering Tycho's letter and the Mechanica, explains why Tengnagel could not convey the secret commission, and accounts for the ensuing delay in replying.
Acknowledges receipt of two letters and the Bavarian library catalogue, explaining his delayed reply by his busy correspondence while sending his eldest son to retrieve instruments from Magdeburg.
Brief maternal letter expressing gladness that Tycho has found settled circumstances, reporting her own good health, and commending him and his household to God.
Thanks Tycho for his letter reporting good circumstances with the Emperor, and explains why he cannot promptly repay the money owed at the current Umschlag.
Explains his delay in replying after returning from the English Legation, and rebukes Tycho for carping at innocent friends through jest and play.
Reports arranging an open boat to transport Tycho's instruments from Hven to Lübeck after a large ship proved impractical due to their size.
Apologizes for delayed reply, excuses Kepler regarding Ursus's insertion of his letter, and describes the disruption caused by relocating his affairs to Bohemia.
Invokes their old Basel friendship and requests a catalogue of the Imperial Library in Vienna, especially its philosophical and mathematical holdings.
Thanks Tycho for past benefits and explains a year's silence caused by domestic troubles and a false rumour of his death circulating at Carnival.
Congratulates Tycho on his imperial patronage and describes Jacob Kindler, a Silesian alchemist at Zittau practising a Paracelsian art of transmuting metals into stones.
Reports receiving Herwart's latest brief letter just before the winter solstice and thanks him for patience with delayed replies and continued friendship.
Acknowledges a letter brought by Kepler on his arrival with Baron Hoffmann, and mentions failed earlier correspondence sent from Wandsbek to Jutland.
Acknowledges letters received via Petkum, gives multiple postal routes for future correspondence, and relays thanks to Burgomaster Möller regarding the Emperor's letter to Hamburg.
Petitions the Emperor to pay over a year's arrears of salary from Bohemian lordships on a quarterly schedule and remedy other outstanding deficiencies.
Reports that Tengnagel twice failed to meet Pinelli in Padua — on the return, Galileo Galilei reported Pinelli had retired — and now writes directly.
Acknowledges Magini's letters via Tengnagel, encloses a brief account of his departure from Denmark and added verses, and urges prompt completion of a promised task.
Confirms receipt of Tycho's Benátky design, reports it will be presented to Barvitius for the Emperor, and relays that Rudolf asks daily after Tycho.
Rebukes Scultetus for persistent failure to reply to letters and explains that the first volume of the Progymnasmata cannot yet be sent as printing is incomplete.
Returns Tobias Fischer's poem with minor corrections and asks Monau to share the revised version with Fischer, noting difficulty locating letters amid the move.
Thanks his uncle Tycho for years of kindness, excuses tardy correspondence by preparations for a study-tour that began 13 December, and promises more regular letters.
Thanks Bachazek for hospitality to his countryman, acknowledges correction of an epigram misprint, and recommends a young Dane newly arrived at Benátky.
Responds to the Emperor's request for a yearly forecast on epidemic diseases by explaining his reservations about astrological prediction and its dependence on lower causes.
Thanks the Grand Duke for his unsolicited letter and expresses pleasure that so eminent a prince takes an interest in astronomy.
Congratulates Hoffmann on his safe return from Austria and expresses confidence in his benevolent support for astronomical studies.
Reports receiving Kepler's letter and urges him to travel at once to Benátky, noting a previous reply was sent via Blotius in Vienna.
Acknowledges Tycho's letter, accepts its excessive praise with humility, and commends the character and bearing of Franz Tengnagel.
Reports holding two letters from David Fabricius and describes a routing plan to forward them via Leipzig and Dresden.
Responds to his nephew's letter, reports his son's return with instruments from Denmark, and plans to send a recommendation for Tage's stay in Basel.
Reports that the runaway Transylvanian has asked forgiveness, wishes Tycho good health after plague in Bohemia, and hopes theological disputes have subsided.
Acknowledges a confidential commission, reports arranging the translation of some eight German letters into Latin, and discusses assistance from a Transylvanian student.
Sends commendatory poems prompted by Taubmann and Brasch, reports learning of Tycho's difficulties with the Danish chancellor, and notes Tycho's kinsman is studying in Heidelberg.
Thanks Hoffmann for his courteous reception of Tengnagel and his son Tycho, and introduces Kepler by praising his mathematical genius.
Sends Tengnagel to expedite business at the Cologne electoral court, describing his household background, travels in Italy, and command of Latin and French.
Rejoices at Coraduz's safe return from Italy and recounts his own arrival in Bohemia in July upon the Emperor's summons.
Apologizes for a delayed reply, attributing it to travel and lack of a reliable courier, and sends Tengnagel to petition the Elector of Cologne.
Notes a previous letter sent via cousin Claude Bille and commends Tengnagel, traveling to the Frankfurt fair before returning to his homeland in Westphalia.
Sends Tengnagel on his journey home, requesting that the recipient support his renewed approach to the Elector of Cologne.
Explains his failure to locate Tycho after Wittenberg, describes false reports that Tycho had settled in Silesia, and mentions Longomontanus as his informant.
Apologizes for a delayed reply due to tertian fever and a printer's uncertainty about paper, expresses joy at Tycho's imperial establishment, and relays Fischer's thanks.
Expresses joy at learning through Monau that his unsolicited letter was well received and that Tycho has admitted him to his circle of friends.
Reports receiving the recipient's letter via son Tyge and notes that her son Tage, sent to Heidelberg for advancement, has written to say he fares well.
Reports stable conditions in Bohemia, notes the Emperor has been absent from Prague for six months due to epidemic sickness, and hopes for improvement.
Wishes the recipient's wife Elisabeth a recovery from her head ailment and reports on a severe pestilence and bloody flux that struck Bohemia the past year.
Thanks his mother for money given to son Tyge, who fashioned a gold bracelet from it to wear in her memory, and reports his situation in Bohemia.
Asks about plans for his nephew Otto — court service or further study — and requests that Otto write to him directly in Latin.
Reports stable conditions in Bohemia, notes the Emperor has been absent from Prague for six months due to epidemic sickness, and expects his return after Easter.
Reports that the recipient's son Claus has left for France to learn the language, as Italian and Spanish now predominate over French at the imperial court.
Instructs that funds held for the Brandenburg mathematician Müller be used to cover messenger expenses, and asks whether letters have arrived from Lübeck, Hamburg, or Wittenberg.
Apologizes for long silence, expresses condolences for the recipient's two lost sons, and requests that he write with news whenever a messenger passes.
Reports arrival in Pilsen to pursue his father's long legal case at court, noting that Tycho's name alone opens ready access to imperial councillors.
Acknowledges the recipient's reproach over long silence in correspondence, defends his familiar style of address toward friends, and thanks him for hospitality shown to his son.
Asks the recipient to send at least his completed work on the three superior planets' orbits under the triple hypotheses, for inclusion in the second Book of Letters.
Reports that the epidemic has subsided and the Emperor lingers at Pilsen but is expected soon in Prague, and discusses an untrustworthy Transylvanian who had sought his letters.
Asks the recipient to investigate the contents of a suppressed supplication by Ursus the Dithmarsian, which complained against him to imperial councillors but was ignominiously rejected.
Returns a corrected sheet for inclusion in the recipient's annual histories, revising the account of being summoned to Bohemia and received by the Emperor.
Thanks an anonymous correspondent for congratulations on his imperial appointment and reflects on divine providence in securing a tranquil harbour after difficulties in his homeland.
Excuses a Livonian correspondent's long silence, offers intercession at the imperial court on his behalf, and welcomes his son's future visit.
Promises to inquire about a Paracelsian chemist in Silesia through Hagecius, and asks the recipient to describe his chemical artifice for extracting something from Bohemian garnets.
Thanks Brasch for congratulations on his imperial appointment and for an elegiac poem featuring Urania, then criticises the poem's polish as inferior to his earlier verse.
Acknowledges Bording's report that Duke Ulrich received news of his imperial position graciously, and notes that subsequent letters from Bording and Henrik Ramel have not arrived.
Apologises for his recent intemperance during his stay at Benátky, recounting Tycho's liberal hospitality and shared observations, and expressing remorse for his conduct.
Thanks Cramer for an ode to the Emperor and pledges to support his bid for the imperial laurel, noting the Emperor's absence from Prague due to plague in Bohemia.
Sends Frankfurt spring fair book catalogues and several books, including works by Gemma Frisius, Camerarius, Peurbach emended by Orontius Finaeus, and the Tables of Queen Elizabeth of England.

documents.recipient_key: The chapter at the cathedral of Magdeburg
documents.abstract: Requests the Chapter's assistance in transferring his astronomical instruments from Magdeburg to Bohemia via the Elbe, the Magdeburg Senate having twice refused the Emperor's letters on the matter.
Reports having assisted a Hamburg citizen through court intermediaries at Rollenhagen's request, and says no further solicitation of the Senate is needed since the Emperor has intervened directly.

Formally acknowledges his arrival at Benátky on 4 February 1600, Tycho's hospitality, and the sharing of observations and astronomical labours, committing to confidentiality regarding the material shared.
Reports that Kepler is departing for Prague before affairs concerning his appointment are concluded at Pilsen, and awaits the Emperor's response to his petitions before settling the matter.
Asks Jessenius to return documents held for Hoffmann and to forward Tengnagel's letters to Daniel so he can solicit Tycho's affairs with both Coraduz and Barvitius.
Warns of postal negligence in Prague and asks Tycho to route future letters through Alexander Prandtl or Johann Menhard rather than the postmaster, to ensure reliable delivery.
Thanks Concini for conveying the Grand Duke of Tuscany's letter and pledges to visit Prague once instrument installations at Benátky and pending observations are attended to.
Thanks Ciaparenius for conveying letters from the Florentine Ambassador and for his kindness to Tengnagel and Tycho's son, and anticipates founding a personal friendship when visiting Prague.
Promises to write to his Lübeck factor to pursue Susanne's debtor David Heidler on her behalf, and asks for news of her husband Dr. Thaddaeus Hájek's health.
Sends several books Tycho requested, including the Prutenic Tables and Copernicus On Triangles, and reports manuscript exemplars of Hipparchus and Ptolemy's Great Syntaxis available for collation.
Thanks Winshemius for repeated correspondence and reports having interceded with Lord Barvitius through Tengnagel on behalf of a Hamburg citizen Winshemius had commended.
Explains his methods for astrological Directions and the distribution of the Heaven, arguing they must be calculated to the Horizon of the native's birthplace rather than current residence.
Reports that kinsman Eske Bille failed to redeem a Holstein bond on time but will settle at the next Umschlag, asking her to secure patience from Dincklage.
Congratulates Moller on his elevation to the Hamburg consulship and urges him to use his authority to intercede in releasing Tycho's instruments and goods held at Lübeck per the Emperor's wishes.
Sends two books by François Viète and reports plans to travel to Augsburg to seek out posthumous manuscript works of Cyprian Leovitius and transmit them to Tycho.
Reports not receiving Tycho's earlier letters or meeting Tengnagel; asks Tycho to repeat their contents; offers assistance and provides a safe Prague address for future correspondence.
Addresses Archduke Matthias, citing his reputed esteem for mathematics, and recalls tokens of favour shown during the Archduke's earlier passage through Denmark.
Responds to Concini's condition regarding the Catholic religion for his son's entry into the Tuscan court, promising the young man will cause no religious offence to anyone.
Initiates correspondence with Galileo after hearing praise of his mathematical abilities from the Tuscan ambassador Concini during a meeting in Prague, seeking to establish a scholarly friendship.
Acknowledges receipt of Tycho's April letter, expresses relief that none of their letters have been lost, and anticipates receiving Tycho's revised lunar hypothesis.
Thanks Christian II for past kindnesses including a gold chain and an invitation at Torgau, and presents him with a star-table inscribed on parchment, sent via Jessenius.
Reports a failed attempt to meet Coraduz in Prague and presses for confirmation of imperial grants promised through Tengnagel's intercession before his departure.
Presses Barvitius to resolve pending matters at the imperial court, having waited fruitlessly in Prague for an audience, and sends a servant to facilitate proceedings.
Sends Jessenius a globe for the Elector of Saxony and a star-table inscribed on parchment, requesting that he deliver both to the Elector on Tycho's behalf.
Reports Carl von Wartenberg's visit and requests to know which Pentecost day Wartenberg has proposed for their joint meeting so Tycho can prepare for the journey.
Reports his prosperous condition in Bohemia under imperial protection and offers assistance at the imperial court, directing Wolframsdorf to Jessenius for fuller particulars.
Reports long-frustrated attempts to reach Tycho by letter from Rostock and later Germany, and expresses joy on learning of his arrival in Prague under imperial patronage.
Thanks Tycho for benefits received, especially for influencing his father's decision to invest in serious study, and pledges lasting gratitude and diligence in return.
Asks an anonymous imperial patron to help a young Danish nobleman of the Rosenkrantz family obtain a military position at the court of Archduke Matthias.
Declines a Whitsun invitation from Berbisdorf, explaining a prior commitment to visit Carl von Wartenberg and Ehrenfried von Minckwitz during the same period.

Discusses printing arrangements for his works, noting Wittenberg or Leipzig as cheaper alternatives to the current printer's excessive price, and briefly acknowledges letters from Fischer and Scultetus.
Apologizes for delayed replies to two letters and enclosed poems, attributing the silence to occupations and changes of place, and thanks Fischer for his sincere affection.
Invokes their old Uraniborg acquaintance and asks Bucretius to help locate a Breslau figure known to have been devoted to astronomy or judicial astrology.
Certifies that Kepler spent four months (February–May 1600) at Benátky working diligently on astronomical exercises with Tycho's instruments and observations.
Confirms receipt of Tycho's May letter, concedes that cheaper printing is available elsewhere than Breslau, and relays greetings from Bucretius.
Reports that the Magdeburg canons are ready to purchase Tycho's astronomical equipment and that two boatmen offer to ship it to Leitmeritz, pressing for a reply.
Thanks Scaliger for his March letter, reports being summoned to Prague by Emperor Rudolf II, and mentions a chance meeting with Nicolaus Suckerback of Meissen, newly arrived from Italy.
Thanks the recipient for an ox procured on his behalf, acknowledges property arrangements in their charge, and promises to send someone to inspect around St. Bartholomew's.
Reports that the printer of Ursus's unauthorized writing is unknown, promises investigation and punishment, and advises Tycho to press the Lord Court-Marshal, under whose jurisdiction Ursus falls.
Certifies that Friedrich Rosenkrantz has been promised a place among Archduke Matthias's attendants and is currently serving under Colonel Kollonitsch before Pápa.
Thanks Holger for his long-awaited letter, acknowledges his reports of Tycho's standing with Emperor Rudolf II, and notes that affairs remain unchanged pending the Emperor's return.
Certifies that Longomontanus served eight years as his astronomical assistant in Denmark, then in Germany and Bohemia, and is now freely dismissed to return home.
Acknowledges payment for a solar and lunar ephemeris sent in March, explains an omission in his earlier letter, and proposes to serve Tycho astronomically from Wittenberg.
Accepts Tycho's criticism of an elegiac poem written in his honour, acknowledging that it lacked the usual finish and polish.
Explains a three-week absence at a Dithmarsian juridical assembly summoned by the Danish king, thanks God for Tycho's health, and pledges assistance regarding Prince Otto of Brunswick.
Explains the delay in reply, reports being summoned from Benátky to Prague for a private audience with Emperor Rudolf II, and begins narrating what has since transpired.
Apologizes for infrequent replies to Herwart's many letters, explains the delay by work on the restitution of the lunar hypothesis, and promises to address Herwart's doubts.
Recounts earlier failed efforts to obtain a laudatory poem from Philipp Menzel in Tycho's honour, and announces that he has now succeeded in procuring one, sent herewith.
Reports delivering the *Mechanica* to Philipp Eduard Fugger at Augsburg and transmits Kepler's earlier letter on Tycho's hypotheses, noting that Ursus, who arrogated them, is now dead.
Replies hastily about revisions to Brasch's Elegiac poem and reports being summoned from Benátky to Prague by the Emperor, who desires him to remain there permanently.
Presses Bording for a third time to procure the money owed by the princes' treasurer and have it sent to Prague in gold or silver coin.
Repeats his request that certain matters be inserted in the late David Chytraeus's annual chronicle, which he expects a Rostock professor to continue through year's end.
Presses Jöstel to send the collation of the Hypotheses with assigned diagrams and adequate explanation, and asks what the printer and Master Oswald will undertake.
Excuses his delayed replies and reports dispatching the six hundred thalers owed to Tycho to Backmeister at Rostock, though the treasurer declined to pay in gold coin.
Acknowledges two letters about Tycho's money owed, reports advising Bording to act on the matter, and mentions the death of Duke Sigismund August of Mecklenburg.
Chides Taubmann in verse for silence and owed poems, encloses verses by Melissus and a heroic poem from an Ingolstadt doctor received via Herwart von Hohenburg.
Agrees that Melissus's recent poems lack their usual polish, defers to Tycho on publication of the Elegy, and reports efforts with Chytraeus's sons about Tycho's chronicle entry.
Sends two books Tycho requested: the Works of Apollonius of Perga and the astronomical tables of Blanchinus, Prugner, and Peurbach.

documents.recipient_key: The dean of the chapter at the cathedral of Magdeburg
documents.abstract: Thanks the Chapter for forwarding his stored goods from Magdeburg to Prague at their own expense, noting the Emperor received this service with favour.
Acknowledges Duke Otto of Brunswick's requests, encloses a reply for him, and reports his instruments installed in an Italian-style house beside the Emperor's garden at Prague.
Reports his goods arrived in Bohemia and asks Rollenhagen to deliver the enclosed letter to the Dean, explaining that the earlier silence was due to pressing imperial duties.
Urges completion of the promised collation, asks what Master Oswald and the printer will undertake, and reports arranging instruments in a new house the Emperor can visit.

documents.recipient_key: The dean and doctors at the college of medicine i Wittenberg
documents.abstract: Declines the invitation to the medical doctoral promotion at Wittenberg, citing his obligations to install his astronomical instruments in a new house at Prague by imperial command.
Sets out the terms of their contract — two years of astronomical assistance with Imperial backing — and reviews grievances arising from his current situation in Bohemia.
Reports finding errors in his own calculations from Tycho's worked examples and marvels that Tycho's eclipse calculation of 10 July agrees with observation to within one arc-minute.
Uses Bopenhausen's return to greet the Landgrave, acknowledges the late Landgrave Wilhelm's past favour, and affirms his continued wish to be of service to Hesse-Kassel.
Reports receiving Bording's reply on 600 joachimsthalers owed by the Mecklenburg treasury, now held by Lucas Backmeister until Gödelmann's arrival.
Reports that Backmeister has received the 600 thalers owed and requests Meier to deliver the next 600 thalers to Gödelmann before his departure to Rostock.
Thanks Bille for redeeming a Holstein bond and requests him to ensure the 10,000-thaler principal is recovered from Mecklenburg rent-master Andreas Meier by April 1601.
Discusses Swedish and Livonian affairs and leaves to Sturtz's judgement what the late Chytraeus wished inserted in the Historiola, with Gödelmann carrying the relevant documents.
Acknowledges agreement on poems by Melissus and Brasch, noting that Gödelmann carries a copy of what Chytraeus wished to insert about his emigration from Denmark.
Requests more rigorous presentation of planetary hypotheses, specifying that Ptolemaic/Alphonsine and Copernican data each be used according to their own parameters.
Reports that Warszewicki did not arrive, expresses concern for Kepler's lack of a secure position, promises to seek astronomical tables, and sends works by Angelus.
Sends the Alphonsine Tables and a transcription of Methodius's Revelation, expressing admiration for Tycho's new solar and lunar calculation.
Writes via his son accompanying Anthony Sherley's Persian legation to Rome, thanks Magini for handling a confidential commission, and discusses Baldi of Urbino's proposed writing project.
Introduces his son Tycho, accompanying Anthony Sherley's Persian legation to Italy, and commends him to the Grand Duke's favour.
Explains delay in carrying out Tycho's undisclosed commission, citing reliance on third parties such as Sagredo and the press of domestic obligations.
Reports Gödelmann's arrival with word that Tycho received his poem fragment, and asks why the promised materials needed to continue the poem were not sent.
Reports Duke Charles's occupation of almost all Livonia, the Polish Diet's resolution to wage war for three years, and personal losses from these events.
Reports paying out 600 thalers to Gödelmann on Tycho's behalf, exchanging Belgian for imperial coin, and notes the other 600 thalers will be due at Easter.
Introduces the bearer as an experienced spagyrist and reports political news about Duke Charles of Sweden's dispute with Lübeck and the recent Polish Diet at Warsaw.
Advocates for publication of an unfinished horological work held by a widow, requesting Tycho's name and patronage to bring it to press.
Announces the planned wedding of his daughter Elisabeth Brahe to Frans Tengnagel at the Curtius house in Prague between Easter and Pentecost, and invites Rosenkrantz.
Reports persistent efforts to obtain imperial intercession through Vice-Chancellor Coraduz on behalf of Rosenkrantz's cousin, delayed by matters of greater state importance.
Reports the Emperor's continued imperial favour and the recent purchase of a large house for 10,000 thalers for his use and astronomical study.
Follows up on a request to have household goods moved from Lübeck to Hamburg and raises the matter of recovering money from the treasurer of the younger Mecklenburg princes.

Sends a copied excerpt on the history of astronomy and directs Brasch to Apian's Astronomicum Caesareum, Reinhold's tables, and Peucer's Sphaera for further sources, leaving composition of a poem to his discretion.
Thanks Bacmeister for transmitting 600 thalers in interest from the Mecklenburg treasurer and presses for repayment of the outstanding principal via Duke Ulrich's authority as guarantor.

Thanks Sturtz for writing and reports political and military news: the Wallachian's new vassal status under the Emperor, Báthory's invasion of Transylvania, and preparations for the renewed Hungarian war.
Announces the betrothal of his daughter Elisabeth Brahe to Frans Tengnagel and invites Duke Ulrich to the planned wedding between Easter and Pentecost.
Reports forwarding Petkum's reply via a student carrier, notes furnaces from Hamburg delayed by Elbe flooding, and encloses a prognostication on the Turkish war by Dethard Horst.
Relays his son's report that the Grand Duke dissuaded the Persian Legation leader from bringing the son to Rome, citing danger from rumours about Tycho already circulating in Italy.

Describes David Fabricius's visit and his observations, laments Fabricius's pastoral constraints, and reports the Bishop of Cologne's mission to the Emperor concerning election of a King of the Romans.
Complains of an unreceived letter and presses Meier for overdue repayment of 10,000 thalers and interest, noting the sum has been pledged to others and kinsman Eske Bille has given assurances.
Müller acknowledges completing one year of imperial-commanded service with Tycho at Prague and records his petition to the Emperor for an honorarium covering expenses and trouble.
Presses again for repayment of 10,000 thalers and interest from the young Mecklenburg dukes, noting Duke Ulrich's prior order to rent-master Meier at Easter has gone unfulfilled.
Inquires whether David Fabricius arrived safely after departing with fears about the dangers of the journey, and commends himself as a friend.
Confirms the 10,000 thalers owed to Tycho fell due at Easter, explains the rent-master's failure to secure promised funds at the last hour, and assures Eske Bille repayment will be arranged.
Recounts successive failed repayment deadlines for the 10,000 thalers owed by Mecklenburg, including the recently-passed Midsummer term, and presses Meier for immediate settlement.
Renews the demand for repayment of 10,000 thalers and interest from Mecklenburg, recounting the contract terms and the loss caused by failure to pay at the agreed Easter deadline.
Explains that the 10,000 thalers have been lying ready in Güstrow since before Midsummer, and that Tycho need only send to demand them against return of the issued bond.
Denies any application for 2,000 thalers at Doberan, reaffirms the earlier call-in of the 10,000 thalers, and recounts the failure of his servant to collect the sum at Easter.
Reports receiving Tycho Brahe's letter claiming 10,000 thalers were paid on St. John's Day, and denies knowledge of a 2,000-thaler demand at Duke Ulrich's court.
Encloses Eske Bille's letter on 10,000 thalers owed to Tycho Brahe, confirms the sum is ready, and questions a report of 5,000 thalers remitted to Prague.
